verses.translation_literal: A song of the ascents. When YHWH returned the returning of Zion, we were like [those who] dream.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song for the climbing road. When the LORD turned Zion's exiles home, when he brought back the ones who return, we could not trust our own eyes. We walked like sleepers, like people moving inside a dream.
verses.directors_commentary:
Don't play this as a victory march; play it as vertigo. The verse opens with a title, 'Song of the Ascents' (KJV 'Song of degrees', which is the Latin gradus, 'steps', and tells a modern reader nothing). It names a group of fifteen psalms, 120 to 134, and the likeliest setting is pilgrims climbing up to Jerusalem for the festivals, singing as they go. The actors are pilgrims, so they sing this on the road, with the city still ahead of them.

The Hebrew plays on one root twice: be-shuv YHWH et-shivat Zion, 'when YHWH returned the returning of Zion'. The KJV's 'turned again the captivity' does two things at once. It chooses one meaning of shivat (captivity, as in the Qere/Ketiv of verse 4) and erases the repetition, so the audience no longer hears the sound of return doubled. Radak takes the verb as transitive ('when YHWH brings back'), Meiri allows a reading in which the line means 'when YHWH returns'; Ibn Ezra reads shivat as a form like shevut. In every case the singer's point is that homecoming and reversal of fortune are one event. The tense is also open: 'we were like dreamers' can be a past memory of the return from Babylon (the 530s BCE), or, as Rashi, Meiri and Malbim read it, the exile's confident vision of a return still to come, as certain as if it had happened. Keep both alive: the actors speak in the past tense, but the dream is not finished.

'Like dreamers' is deliberately ambiguous too: people who cannot believe what they see, or people whose longing has been so strong that they have already dreamed it (Malbim, citing Jeremiah 31:26).

philological_notes.note: 'The ascents' (the KJV 'degrees' comes from the Latin gradus). The word is from the root 'to go up', and the commonest explanation is pilgrim songs for the climb to Jerusalem; the Mishnah (Middot, Sukkah) ties it to the fifteen steps of the Temple, which is a later tradition. The packet's commentaries do not explain the title beyond Ibn Ezra's comparison with 'song of the Most High'.

Root play: 'in YHWH's returning the returning of Zion'. Shivat is read by Ibn Ezra as shaped like shevut (captivity), so 'restored fortunes' and 'returned exiles' are both heard; Zion may be the people or the city.

'Like dreamers': either dazed disbelief at the sudden good news, or the longing of exiles who dreamed of home (the verb can also mean 'to be restored to health', Isaiah 38:16, which some readers hear here; that is my reading and carries no source).

verses.translation_literal: Then our mouth was filled [with] laughter, and our tongue [with] a ringing cry; then they said among the nations, "YHWH has made great to do with these."
verses.translation_dramatic: Then laughter filled our mouths to the brim, and our tongues rang with song. Then, among the nations, voices said it too: "The LORD has done something great for these people."
verses.directors_commentary:
The mouth and the tongue are the whole body of the singers: laughter fills the mouth and has to spill out. The verb is the Hebrew yimmale, 'was filled', in a form that can be read as past or as the future the singers already taste; the KJV's 'filled with laughter' is fine, but 'singing' for rinnah is soft. Rinnah is a ringing shout, a cry that carries across a valley, the sound of a crowd at a harvest or a victory, not a hymn in a pew.

The second half moves the audience outward. 'They said among the nations' puts the foreigners in the scene as witnesses, and they speak the line that the singers repeat in verse 3: 'YHWH has made great to do'. The KJV's 'the Lord hath done great things for them' smooths an odd Hebrew phrase, higdil la'asot, literally 'made great to act', into plain English. The point is the note of surprise: in the ancient Near East the god of a defeated people was counted defeated with them, so that the nations notice a reversal and credit it to the god of the losers is itself a reversal. 'Nations' (goyim) is the KJV's 'heathen', which adds a religious sneer the Hebrew does not have.

Ibn Ezra notes that 'our mouth' is singular for a plural people, like 'our soul' in Psalm 124:7: one voice for the whole crowd.

philological_notes.note: A ringing cry of joy, a shout carried by the voice; 'singing' (KJV) is too gentle. The same word returns in verses 5 and 6, so the psalm's joy is one sound heard three times.
'He made great to do': an idiom for a mighty deed, with the verb 'made great' left bare. Metzudat David says the point is that these great things come from YHWH and not by chance.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH has made great to do with us; we were joyful.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD has done great things with us, and we, we were wild with joy.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the singers take the foreigners' sentence out of their mouths and say it in their own voice. The same four words as in verse 2, higdil YHWH la'asot, but one word changes: 'with these' becomes 'with us' (immanu). Play the change: first heard from outside, now owned. This is the hinge of the psalm.

The last words, hayinu semehim, 'we were joyful', are a verb of being plus an adjective. The KJV's 'whereof we are glad' invents a present tense and a 'whereof' that the Hebrew does not have, and so turns an outburst into a tidy conclusion. The Hebrew perfect fits the memory of the return or, as Meiri reads it, the confident language of prophecy, where the future is told in the past tense. The ambiguity is left open on purpose, because verse 4 will turn out to ask for the restoration again.

philological_notes.note: 'With us'; the word recalls 'Immanuel' and plays against 'with these' in verse 2. The Hebrew preposition 'im is 'with', not 'for' as in KJV, and so keeps the sense that God acted in company with his people.

verses.translation_literal: Return, O YHWH, [obj] our captivity, like stream-beds in the Negev.
verses.translation_dramatic: Turn it back, LORD. Bring home our captives and our lost fortunes, as the dry riverbeds of the Negev fill with sudden water.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood breaks. After three verses of memory, the singers now ask, with the imperative shuvah, 'return!': the same root as in verse 1, but now spoken to God. The joy of the dream was not yet the whole thing. Whether the first half is a flashback to the return from Babylon and this is a prayer for the people still scattered or still impoverished, or whether it is the exiles' anticipation, the prayer fits either. Radak and Metzudat David say the exiles speak these words while still in exile.

The simile is the key. An afiq is not a 'stream' (KJV) with a quiet flow but a stream-bed or wadi. In the Negev, the dry south of Judah, these channels are dust for most of the year, then in the rainy winter a storm far off in the hills sends a flash flood down them within minutes, and the desert turns green. The KJV's 'streams in the south' lets a modern reader picture a brook. Play it as a sudden miracle: what was dead is suddenly rushing. Ibn Ezra and Meiri stress the strength of the flow; Radak, the contrast with the dry land.

Textual note: the written text has shevutenu, the reading tradition shevitenu; Radak and Meiri say they mean the same. 'Captivity' (shevut) can also mean 'fortunes', which is why modern versions such as BBE say 'fate'.

philological_notes.note: The Ketiv (written) is שבותנו, the Qere (read) שביתנו. Radak and Meiri report it and say the sense is the same. The noun is tied to 'captivity' (shevi) but also to the 'returning' of the root shuv, so 'restore our fortunes' is a legitimate rendering.
Channels, stream-beds, wadis that carry water seasonally; the KJV 'streams' loses the dry/flood contrast.
The Negev, the dry south; the word also means 'south' and is tied by Ibn Ezra and Meiri to nagav, 'dry' (compare Targum nigevu mayya, 'the waters dried up'). KJV 'the south' hides the proper name.

verses.translation_literal: Those who sow with a tear [will] reap with a ringing cry.
verses.translation_dramatic: Those who sow in tears will reap with a shout of joy.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a proverb, and the best way to play it is as one: short, balanced, and said slowly. It is the farmer's image applied to the exiles. In dry country like the Negev, sowing is a gamble: if the rains fail, the seed is lost, so a poor farmer sows in tears, as Radak and Metzudat David say, because he fears the seed will not sprout. The rains, the flood in the wadis of verse 4, change everything.

The Hebrew has a wordplay that no English version keeps: be-dim'ah, 'with a tear' (singular, one tear after another) against be-rinnah, 'with a ringing cry', the joy word of verses 2 and 6. The KJV's 'in tears... in joy' is correct but flat; the Hebrew puts two single words side by side, a tear and a shout. The classical tradition, Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak, read the sowing as keeping the commandments in exile and the reaping as the reward; the actors do not need to settle that, but should know the field is also a moral image.

philological_notes.note: 'With a tear', singular; paired with rinnah to make a sharp contrast of two sounds, weeping and the joyful cry.

verses.translation_literal: Going he will go, and weeping, carrying the seed-bag; coming he will come with a ringing cry, carrying his sheaves.
verses.translation_dramatic: He goes out, he keeps going, weeping, with the seed-bag on his shoulder. He will come home, he will surely come home, with a shout of joy, his arms full of sheaves.
verses.directors_commentary:
Verse 5 stated the rule; verse 6 shows one man doing it, in a film-like pair of shots. Outgoing: the farmer walks out to the field, weeping, carrying the seed. Returning: he walks the same road home, singing, carrying grain. The Hebrew builds both halves with the same device, an infinitive absolute before the verb: halokh yelekh, 'going he will go', and bo yavo, 'coming he will come'. The KJV's 'shall doubtless come again' captures the certainty but loses the doubled motion, the long walk out and the long walk back. The chiasm is the point: nose'... nose'; 'carrying the seed-bag' at the start, 'carrying his sheaves' at the end, with the same participle, so the load in his arms is the only thing that changes.

The seed-bag is uncertain. Meshekh ha-zara' is 'the bag of seed' for Ibn Ezra and Meiri (a vessel the sower carries), 'precious seed' for Radak, who derives it from a root meaning 'to draw out', and that is how the KJV got 'precious seed'. Metzudat Zion takes it as 'drawing, carrying'. I read the carried object as a container because the participle is 'carrying'. The weeping is the sower's fear for the seed in dry soil (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri), not a funeral.

A sheaf (alummah) is a bundle of cut grain tied up by the reapers, the same word as in Joseph's dream in Genesis 37:7, and shows the harvest in a visible, concrete shape. Rashi, Radak and Meiri read the whole verse as a figure for exile and reward; Malbim, for a surprise greater than the exiles dared hope.

philological_notes.note: Disputed: 'seed-bag' (Ibn Ezra, Meiri: the vessel in which seed is carried), 'precious seed' (Radak, who ties it to the root 'to draw'), or 'the carrying of the seed' (Metzudat Zion, Metzudat David). The context of 'carrying' favors a container.
Infinitive absolute with the finite verb: an emphatic or continuing action. Echoed in bo yavo ('he will surely come'). Translations such as the KJV render only the second, 'doubtless come again'.
'His sheaves', bundles of cut grain; the word is found in Joseph's dream of binding sheaves (Genesis 37:7), as Metzudat Zion points out.
